Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:35: "You shall surely give him, and your heart shall not be grieved when you give to him" (Deuteronomy 15:10). We have been warned by this to remove from our soul a stingy eye and to become good of eye, as it is said (Proverbs 22:9), "He who has a good eye shall be blessed." And it is not enough to give with the hand until we have planted in our souls the trait of generosity; therefore Scripture warned and said, "and your heart shall not be grieved," after already saying, "You shall surely give him."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:36: "You shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand" (Deuteronomy 15:7). We have been warned by this to remove from our soul the trait of cruelty, and to plant in it pleasant plantings, namely mercy and faithful kindnesses, as it is written (ibid. v. 5[?]), "and you shall walk in His ways." And because it is possible that a man might not shut his hand and might favor the poor man, yet not out of a way of compassion — as it is said (Proverbs 12:10), "but the mercies of the wicked are cruel" — therefore it is written, "You shall not harden your heart." And the punishment of cruelty is evil and bitter, as will be explained, with God's help, in the Gate of Cruelty. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Shabbat 151b), "and show you mercy, and have compassion upon you, and multiply you" — whoever has mercy on creatures, mercy is shown to him from Heaven, and whoever does not have mercy on creatures, no mercy is shown to him from Heaven.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:37: "And your eye shall not pity him, nor shall you spare, nor shall you conceal him" (Deuteronomy 13:9). We have been warned by this not to have pity or mercy on those who cause others to sin and lead them to stumble. And our Sages of blessed memory said: whoever becomes merciful toward the cruel will in the end become cruel toward the merciful.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:38: "You shall not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people" (Leviticus 19:18). Our Sages of blessed memory said: what is vengeance? He says to him, Lend me your axe; he says to him, I will not lend it to you, just as you did not lend me yours. And what is bearing a grudge? He says to him, Here, I will lend it to you, but I am not like you, who did not lend to me. And the punishment here is not for the speech but for the grudge held in the heart. And our Sages of blessed memory said that the warning against bearing a grudge applies to a matter of money, but concerning matters of pride, contempt, and the pursuit of harm, it is permitted for a man to hold the matter in his heart [i.e., to remain wary]. And our Sages of blessed memory said concerning this: any Torah scholar who does not avenge and bear a grudge like a serpent is no scholar; but if forgiveness is sought from him, he should overlook his own attributes [and forgo it].
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:39: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart" (Leviticus 19:17). We have been warned by this to remove from our soul the trait of hatred, which is a trait that brings about many transgressions and gives rise to numerous corrupt practices, such as evil speech, which is weighed as equal to several transgressions liable to death by the court, as will be explained; and such as the pursuit of harm, rejoicing at another's misfortune, causing damage to one's fellows, talebearing, and vengeance and grudge-bearing; and it destroys much good from the soul, as will be explained in the Gate of Hatred. And see to what extent the punishment for hatred reached: for our Sages of blessed memory said, in the Second Temple period, when they were occupied with Torah and good deeds — why was it destroyed? Because of the needless hatred that was among them.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:40: "And you shall guard yourself from every evil thing" (Deuteronomy 23:10). Our Sages, of blessed memory, explained: a man should not entertain lewd thoughts by day and thereby come to impurity at night. This applies even if he does not think of it in order to actually act upon it. And the matter is derived from its context, since it is written afterward (Deuteronomy 23:11), "If there be among you a man who is not clean because of what happens to him at night..."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:41: "And you shall not go about after your heart and after your eyes" (Numbers 15:39). We have been warned by this not to plan to commit a transgression, or any matter of iniquity or sin, as it is said (Proverbs 24:8), "He who plots to do evil..."; and not to entertain the words of heretics, lest he stumble and be drawn after them. And whoever takes to heart that the Blessed Name examines the heart and searches the innermost being — how could he be so brazen as to defile his heart and pour a worthless matter into it? And Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 24:9), "The scheme of folly is sin." He further said (Proverbs 6:16-18), "These six things the Lord hates, and seven are an abomination to His soul: ... a heart that devises wicked thoughts..."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:42: "You shall not accept a false report" (Exodus 23:1). We have been warned by this not to accept evil speech, as the Targum renders it: "You shall not accept a report of falsehood."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:43: "You shall not covet your neighbor's house" (Exodus 20:14), "neither shall you desire your neighbor's house" (Deuteronomy 5:18). We have been warned by this not to scheme wicked schemes to take a field, a vineyard, or anything belonging to our neighbor, even if we pay its price. And we have been warned concerning the very thought of this evil matter, that we should not consent in our thought to do it, as it is said, "You shall not covet." And if a man longs for his fellow to sell him a field, a vineyard, or one of his possessions, he should not press him to sell it; and if he pressures him with many pleading words such that the man is ashamed to refuse him, it is forbidden to pressure him thus, for this is like coercion and force. And whoever covets to take any object, if he is an honored man, such that were he to ask a favor, others would not be able to refuse him for fear of dishonoring him, it is forbidden for him to ask his fellow for a purchase or a gift, unless he knows that the other will give it to him with a willing soul, and his heart will not be grieved when he gives it to him.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:44: Among the warnings that depend on the tongue: "For the Lord your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you and to give up your enemies before you; therefore your camp shall be holy, that He see no unseemly thing among you" (Deuteronomy 23:15). Our Sages, of blessed memory, said that this warning includes the following: that when we meditate on the Torah of the Blessed Name, and when we speak in prayer before Him, our camp should be holy and He should see no unseemly thing among us. Therefore we were commanded by this to mention the Name of Heaven in holiness, and to occupy ourselves with words of Torah and prayer in holiness, and not to mention the Name of Heaven or words of Torah while naked, or if there is a naked person present opposite him. And we were likewise warned that the place be clean, as it is said (Deuteronomy 23:14), "and you shall dig with it, and shall turn back and cover that which comes from you." And how much more is one warned not to mention the Name of Heaven if his hands are not clean; and if his hands have touched something repugnant to him, he should wash them, in the sense of what is said (Psalms 26:6), "I will wash my hands in cleanness." And when walking on a road, if he is in doubt whether the road is clean, he should not mention the Name of Heaven nor speak words of Torah there. And if there is something unclean behind him, such as excrement, carrion, or steeping water, he must distance himself four cubits from the place where the odor ends, and in front of him as far as his eyes can see. And carefulness in this is among the ways of the fear of Heaven, as it is said (Malachi 3:16), "for those who fear the Lord and those who think upon His name." And our Sages of blessed memory said (Numbers 15:31), "because he has despised the word of the Lord" — this refers to one who speaks words of Torah in filthy alleyways. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Ecclesiastes Rabbah 1:7): "He gives wisdom to the wise" — because the wise honor the Torah and occupy themselves with it in holiness; whereas had it been given to fools, they would speak words of Torah in filthy alleyways.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:45: And among the warnings that depend on the tongue, there are some for which one is lashed, for so our Sages of blessed memory said: for all the warnings in the Torah that involve no action, one is not lashed, except for one who swears falsely and one who curses his fellow by the Name. And a vain oath, even though it does not carry death by the court, its punishment at the hand of Heaven is more severe than that of many transgressions which do carry death by the court, for one who swears falsely desecrates the Name, as it is said (Leviticus 19:12), "and you shall not swear by My name falsely, for you would profane the name of your God." And the punishment for desecration of the Name exceeds that of all other transgressions; and this is not written concerning any other transgression except a false oath and idolatry, as it is said (Leviticus 20:3), "because he has given of his offspring to Molech, to defile My sanctuary and to profane My holy name." And it is said in the warnings against idolatry (Exodus 20:5), "You shall not bow down to them, nor serve them, for I the Lord your God am a jealous God" — meaning, that the iniquity of idolatry is not forgiven in the manner of His forgiveness for other transgressions, as it is written (Jeremiah 5:7), "How can I pardon you for this? Your children have forsaken Me and sworn by what is not God." And so it is written in the warnings against a false oath (Exodus 20:7), "for the Lord will not hold him guiltless who takes His name in vain." And the warning against a false oath is written immediately after the warning against idolatry, because a false oath, within its folds, is found to carry the iniquity of desecrating the Blessed Name. And our Sages of blessed memory said, concerning what is written (Proverbs 30:8), "Give me neither poverty nor riches...lest I be full and deny, and say, Who is the Lord? Or lest I be poor and steal, and profane the name of my God" — the second is worse than the first, as it is said (Ezekiel 20:39), "and as for you, O house of Israel...go, serve every one his idols; but afterward, if you will not listen to Me, then you shall no more profane My holy name." Its meaning: the iniquity of one who swears falsely in court is graver than the punishment of one who worships idols in secret, because of the desecration of the Name. And our Sages, of blessed memory, said: for all transgressions in the Torah, retribution is exacted from him and from his family, but here, from him and from the whole world. And if the court obligated a man to take an oath, and he knows that his mouth would speak falsehood, it is forbidden for him to accept the oath upon himself, saying, I will swear in order to frighten my fellow, even though he does not truly intend to swear falsely, as it is said (Exodus 20:7), "You shall not take [in vain]" — and this is included in its implication: you shall not accept to swear falsely. And so our Sages, of blessed memory, said in the Mekhilta; and the Targum of (Exodus 23:1), "You shall not accept a false report," is "you shall not accept." And it is forbidden to swear needlessly, even when swearing to the truth, as it is said (Exodus 20:7), "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain," the Targum rendering it "for nothing." And likewise, one who causes his fellow to swear needlessly, his iniquity is great — such as when his fellow owes him a hundred coins and he doubles his claim so that the line of the law will require, upon the other's partial admission, that he take the Torah-mandated oath; or one who sues his fellow needlessly for something he does not know for certain, and asks him and makes him swear an oath of inducement (heset). And our Sages said that such a man is called a thief, for he steals the minds of people; and of him it is said (Zechariah 5:4), "I will bring it forth, says the Lord of hosts, and it shall enter into the house of the thief, and into the house of him that swears falsely by My name, and it shall remain in the midst of his house, and shall consume it, with its timber and its stones." And one who knows that if he swears, people will suspect him regarding his oath, should refrain and spare his soul from the oath, for the honor of Heaven, even though the truth is with him.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:46: "You shall not curse God, nor curse a ruler of your people" (Exodus 22:27); "You shall not curse the deaf" (Leviticus 19:14). We have been warned by this that a man of Israel should not be cursed by the Name, nor by any of its various appellations. And what the Torah mentions — "You shall not curse God," and a ruler, and the deaf — it comes to warn against cursing the judge when he rules against him in judgment, and against cursing the ruler when he punishes him by delivering him over to the hand of his own transgression. And it was necessary to mention the deaf, lest you say there is no punishment for cursing him, since he does not hear and no distress reaches him from the curse. And at the end of the portion of Mishpatim it is written, "You shall not curse God," meaning: you shall not curse the judge over these very judgments; but a judge who does not judge according to the law, you may curse. And our Sages of blessed memory said: one who curses his fellow or himself by the Name is lashed, and his punishment at the hand of Heaven is very great, as it is said (Deuteronomy 28:58-59), "If you will not observe to do all the words of this Torah... to fear this glorious and awesome Name, the Lord your God, then the Lord will make your plagues wonderful, etc." And our Sages of blessed memory explained the matter of this verse as referring to one who curses his fellow or himself by the Name.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:47: And it is forbidden for a man to say, So may the Name save him, as this matter is true — when in fact it is false; for behold, he has thereby cursed himself by the Name, since from the positive you may infer the negative [i.e., such a formula implies an oath].
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:48: "Drink no wine nor strong drink...and that you may teach the children of Israel" (Leviticus 10:9), "and to distinguish between the holy and the profane." Our Sages of blessed memory said: one who has drunk a quarter-log of undiluted wine should not render halachic rulings; and if he drank more than a quarter-log, even diluted, he should not render rulings.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:49: "You shall not wrong one another" (Leviticus 25:17) — Scripture speaks of wronging through words, as we stated earlier. And our Sages said: if he was a penitent, one should not say to him, Remember your former deeds; if he was the son of converts, one should not say to him, Remember the deeds of your ancestors. And this is what is said (Exodus 22:20), "You shall not wrong a stranger, nor oppress him" — "you shall not wrong" through words, "nor oppress" through money. And in several places the Torah warned against wronging the convert, because he has forgotten his people and his father's house and come to take shelter beneath the wings of the Divine Presence, as it is said (Ruth 2:11), "and you have left your father and your mother and the land of your birth, and have come to a people that you did not know before," and it is said (Ruth 2:12), "and let your reward be complete from the Lord, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge" — a parable of a gazelle that comes to the flock and lies down there and grazes with the sheep, and the owner of the flock has compassion on it, since it left a broad meadow and came to stand in a narrow place.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:50: "You shall not follow the multitude to do evil" (Exodus 23:2). We have been warned by this not to strengthen the hands of transgressors with words, and not to associate with those who consent to injustice, in the sense of what is said (Isaiah 8:12), "Say not, A conspiracy, of all that this people shall call a conspiracy."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:51: And it is forbidden to associate with a wicked man in worldly dealings, as it is said (II Chronicles 20:37), "Because you have joined yourself with Ahaziah, the Lord has broken your works." And it is said (Proverbs 3:31), "Envy not the man of violence, and choose none of his ways." And our Sages of blessed memory said in the Avot of Rabbi Natan: Do not be a companion to a wicked man, even for the sake of a mitzvah, for many are the ways of death found in the company of the wicked. And we have already revealed the nature of this iniquity and the weight of its punishment.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:52: "And you shall not put a stumbling-block before the blind" (Leviticus 19:14). We have been warned by this not to instruct the children of Israel in a manner that is not according to the law and not according to the halachah. And our Sages of blessed memory said: be deliberate in judgment. And those who are hasty of heart to understand and to rule will not save their souls from putting a stumbling-block before the blind, and their sin is exceedingly heavy, as it is said (Psalms 82:5), "They know not, neither do they understand; they walk on in darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken." They further said: be careful in study, for an error in study amounts to a deliberate transgression. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Sotah 22a): "For she has cast down many wounded" — this refers to a student who has not yet reached the level of rendering halachic decisions, yet rules; "and a mighty host are all her slain" — this refers to a student who has reached the level of rendering decisions, yet does not rule.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:53: We are further warned, from this same verse, to give fitting counsel to one who consults with us, and not to cause him to stumble through foolish counsel, and not to counsel one's fellow according to one's own way [rather than his].
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:54: And a man is obligated to devise plans to offer fitting and proper counsel to his fellow; and this is among the essential ways of acts of kindness, as it is said (Proverbs 27:9), "Oil and incense rejoice the heart, and the sweetness of a friend comes from earnest counsel."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:55: "You shall not go about as a talebearer among your people" (Leviticus 19:16). Our Sages of blessed memory said that this warning includes not bringing forth an evil name upon a man of our people, and its punishment at the hand of Heaven is severe, as will be explained at the level of those liable to death. Our Sages of blessed memory further said: "You shall not go about as a talebearer among your people" is also a warning to the judge, that he not be gentle to one litigant and harsh to the other.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:56: "And make no mention of the name of other gods" (Exodus 23:13). A man should not say to his fellow, Wait for me near such-and-such an idol.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:57: "You shall show them no favor" (Deuteronomy 7:2). Our Sages, of blessed memory, explained: you shall not give them favor — for it is forbidden for a man to say, How handsome this gentile is. They further explained it as meaning not to give them a gratuitous gift.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:58: "And that he be not as Korah and his company" (Numbers 17:5). Our Sages of blessed memory said (Sanhedrin 110a): whoever persists in a dispute transgresses a negative commandment, as it is said, "and that he be not as Korah and his company." And it is permitted to speak evil of those who persist in dispute, as it is said (I Kings 1:26), "but me, your servant, and Zadok the priest, etc., he did not invite."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:59: Whoever does not persist in dispute against those who stand firm on a bad path and draw others into iniquity is punished for their transgressions, for all their sins, and transgresses a negative commandment, as it is said (Leviticus 19:17), "and not bear sin because of him." And it is said (Hosea 10:9), "From the days of Gibeah you have sinned, O Israel; there they stood; the battle against the sons of iniquity did not overtake them in Gibeah." Its meaning: if this generation had stood there, the battle to root out evil would not have overtaken them at Gibeah, as it overtook the people of that [earlier] generation — "there they stood" meaning "had they stood there" (a conditional, like other instances in Scripture of an implied "if"). Its meaning is: their sin was of the same kind as the sin of Gibeah; yet they [the men of that earlier generation] were better than these, for they gathered together and stood firm to root out the evil. And it is said (Judges 5:23), "Curse Meroz, said the angel of the Lord, curse bitterly its inhabitants, because they came not to the help of the Lord, to the help of the Lord against the mighty." And it is said (Deuteronomy 1:17), "You shall not be afraid of the face of any man." And whoever belongs to the Blessed Name shall give up his life for the sanctification of the Name, as it is said (Exodus 32:26), "Whoever is for the Lord, come to me — and all the sons of Levi gathered to him," and it is said (Numbers 25:7), "And Pinchas saw... and took a spear in his hand." And it is an obligation upon every God-fearing person, and all the more so upon one who loves Him with a pure heart, to be aroused to zeal when he sees the hand of officers and dignitaries engaged in betrayal. And our Sages of blessed memory said: any breach that does not begin with the great ones is no breach, as it is said (Ezra 9:2), "and the hand of the officers and rulers has been foremost in this treachery."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:60: "But over your brethren, the children of Israel, you shall not rule, one over another, with rigor" (Leviticus 25:46). A man should not enslave his fellows; and if his fear is upon them, or they are ashamed to disregard his word, he should not command them to do anything, small or great, except for their own will and benefit — not even to heat a jug of water or to go on an errand to the city square to buy a loaf of bread. But a man who does not conduct himself properly may be commanded to do whatever one wishes.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:61: "And you shall not profane My holy name" (Leviticus 22:32). This is among the transgressions liable to excision, as will be explained. And know that the loss and destruction found in the souls of the multitude of the people is indeed upon the tip of the tongue, for they mention the Name of Heaven in vain, and mention it even without reverence. And concerning this matter our Sages of blessed memory explained what is written (Isaiah 1:3), "Israel does not know." They are also not scrupulous about the cleanliness of the place or the cleanness of their hands. And the Sages of Israel would place under a ban and excommunicate one who uttered the Name of Heaven in vain, and would suspect him regarding oaths; and they said, one who hears his fellow mentioning the Name of Heaven in vain must place him under a ban, and if he does not do so, he himself falls under the ban.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:62: And concerning people who are not careful with their tongue regarding the honor of Torah scholars, whether in their presence or not in their presence — they become heretics who have no share in the World to Come. And so the destruction of the four factions [mentioned in the Talmud] comes about through the sin of their mouth, the word of their lips — all as will be explained in this Gate. Therefore it is written (Proverbs 18:21), "Death and life are in the hand of the tongue."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:63: And consider and see the iniquity of the tongue and the weight of its transgression: for one who curses his father and mother has a graver punishment than one who strikes them, since the sentence of one who curses is stoning, which is the gravest of the deaths administered by the court, while the sentence of one who strikes is strangulation.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:64: And many, too, are ensnared and trapped by profaning the honored senses — the sense of sight and the sense of hearing. And concerning the sense of sight it is said (Numbers 15:39), "and you shall not go about after your heart and after your eyes." We have been warned by this that a man should not gaze upon a married woman or other forbidden women, lest he be ensnared by them.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:65: And among the transgressions that depend on the sense of sight is haughtiness of the eyes, for it is caused by pride, as it is said (Psalms 101:5), "him that has a haughty eye and a proud heart I will not endure."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:66: And among the words of our Sages concerning the sense of hearing: a man should not let his ears hear worthless matters, for they scorch the limbs first of all. And of one who gives ear to every mouth that speaks vileness it is said (Proverbs 22:14), "The mouth of strange women is a deep pit." Let all God-fearing people and penitents take these things to heart, to save their souls from the hand of the flame; and we have already stated for you honorable words on this matter in the Gates of the Fences of Carefulness.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:67: Among the warnings that depend on the withholding of one's hand and refraining from an action: "You shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother, etc. Take heed lest there be a base thought in your heart, saying, The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand; and your eye be evil against your poor brother, and you give him nothing" (Deuteronomy 15:7-9). From this we learn that one who refrains from lending to the poor transgresses two negative commandments, namely "take heed" and "lest." And if, at a time when the seventh year is near, we have been warned not to refrain from lending out of fear of the matter of release — how much more so at a time when he will not lose his debt, for the sin of one who shuts his hand from lending grows all the greater. And because of the greatness of this iniquity, Scripture calls the thought of a stingy eye toward lending "a base (belial) thought." And our Sages of blessed memory said: whoever hides his eyes from charity is as though he worshipped idols — for here it is written, "lest there be a base thought (davar belial) in your heart," and there (Deuteronomy 13:14) it is written, "certain base men (benei belial) have gone out from among you." And our Sages of blessed memory said that the stingy-eyed man is called "belial." And so it is written (I Samuel 25:25), "to this man of belial, to Nabal" — because he was stingy-eyed, having said to David's servants (I Samuel 25:11), "Shall I then take my bread and my water and my meat, etc." And our Sages of blessed memory said (Shabbat 63a): greater is one who lends to the poor than one who gives charity.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:68: "You shall not oppress your neighbor" (Leviticus 19:13). And David, peace upon him, said (Psalms 37:21), "The wicked borrows, and does not repay." (Leviticus 19:13), "The wages of a hired laborer shall not remain with you all night until morning." (Deuteronomy 24:15), "On his day you shall give him his wages, nor shall the sun go down upon it." And our Sages said (Bava Metzia 110b): a day-laborer may collect his wage the whole day and the whole night [that follows]; a night-laborer may collect his wage the whole night and the whole [following] day. Whether it is the hire of an animal, the wage of a man, or the rental of vessels, one transgresses concerning them the prohibition against delay; and one who contracts for piecework also transgresses concerning it the prohibition against delay.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:69: "His body shall not remain all night upon the tree" (Deuteronomy 21:23). One who leaves his dead unburied overnight transgresses a negative commandment, unless he left him overnight for the sake of his honor.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:70: "You may not hide yourself" (ibid. 22 [Deuteronomy 22:3]). We have been warned by this not to be negligent in saving our fellow's property, whether movable goods or real estate, as our Sages of blessed memory said (ibid.): "and so shall you do with every lost thing of your brother's," to include the loss of real estate — such as, if flowing water was coming to a certain place, one is obligated to build a barrier against it. Moreover, we have been warned to strive to help save our fellow, and to devise plans to assist them in their time of trouble; and so it is written (Leviticus 19:16), "You shall not stand idly by the blood of your neighbor." And Solomon said (Proverbs 24:10), "If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small." Its meaning: if you have the strength to save through counsel or through effort, and you present yourself as though you had no ability — your strength shall become small, measure for measure. And it is said afterward (Proverbs 24:12), "If you say, Behold, we knew it not — does not He who weighs the hearts consider it? And He who guards your soul, does He not know it? And shall He not render to every man according to his work?" Behold, one's refraining from rescue and from devising counsel to help — the Holy One, blessed be He, reckons it to him as though it were his own deed.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:71: And it is good and most proper for there to be, in every single city, volunteers from among the people, from those of understanding, ready and prepared for every matter of rescue, whenever a man or woman of Israel is in distress. And behold, we have been obligated to trouble ourselves even over our brother's stray ox or sheep, to stay with it until our brother comes seeking it — how much more so must we act to preserve the dignity and honor of their owners themselves. And so it is written (Isaiah 58:7), "and that you bring the wandering poor into your house."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:72: "You shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not bear sin because of him" (Leviticus 19:17). We have been warned by this not to bear sin along with our fellow's sin by refraining from rebuking them. And if one man sins, once his sin becomes revealed, the whole congregation will be punished on his account if they do not rebuke him with the rod of their discipline. And so it is written (Joshua 22:20), "Did not Achan the son of Zerah commit a trespass in the devoted thing, and wrath fell upon all the congregation of Israel? And that man did not perish alone in his iniquity." And it is said (Deuteronomy 29:28[29]), "but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever." And even the nations of the world said (Jonah 1:7), "and let us know for whose cause this evil is upon us" — how much more so Israel, who are all sureties one for another.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:73: And in order to be saved from this punishment, it is proper to choose men of truth and to select from among all the people men of valor, to appoint them as heads of oversight over every marketplace and open area of their dwellings, to watch over their neighbors and to rebuke them concerning every matter of transgression, and to root out the evil.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 3:74: "When you make a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not delay to pay it" (Deuteronomy 23:22). Behold, there is a punishment for delaying vows and charitable pledges, even though one pays them afterward. And if a man vowed to give charity to the poor, he is obligated to pay it immediately. And even if delaying the vow happens to him out of forgetfulness, he is nonetheless punished for this, for since he knows that forgetfulness is common among people, he ought to remember his vows and keep them before his heart always, so as not to forget them — as it is said (Proverbs 20:25), "It is a snare for a man rashly to say, It is holy, and only after vows to make inquiry." Therefore his punishment for his negligence is severe, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 5:5), "Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was an error; why should God be angry at your voice, and destroy the work of your hands?" Its meaning: do not let your mouth cause you to sin, etc. — why should you vow, if you are not careful with your vow, and thereby bring guilt upon yourself? And we have already explained this verse earlier, in the Gates of the Fences of Carefulness. And our Sages of blessed memory said: because of the sin of [unfulfilled] vows, children die, as it is said, "and destroy the work of your hands." This verse is also explained as concerning the matter of evil speech, that one is punished for negligence in it even though he did not intend to demean his fellow. And behold, we have been commanded not to make vows, as it is said (Deuteronomy 23:23), "But if you refrain from vowing, it shall be no sin in you" — and our Sages expounded from this that if you do vow, there will be sin in you, for the vow is a stumbling-block before the one who vows, lest he profane his word or delay in paying it. But a righteous man is gracious and gives without vowing, except when he cries out from distress, for then he may make a vow, as in the matter written (Genesis 28:20), "And Jacob vowed a vow, saying, etc." And so, when the heads of the people gather together, the tribes of Israel as one, they may make vows to strengthen weak hands.
